sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
In order to collect energy from human activities, piezoelectric energy harvesters should have a flexible structure, low resonant frequency and wide frequency bandwidth. In this paper, the fabrication and characterization of a metalbased Pb(Zr,Ti)O3 (PZT) bimorph thick film energy harvester. PZT thick films were deposited on cantilever-shaped titanium (Ti) substrate via a dip-coating process. The electrical properties of the PZT films sintered at different temperatures were investigated. The nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester has the following advantages: it is suitable for low frequency, weak vibration, and wide frequency bandwidth. The maximum open-circuit voltage of the piezoelectric energy harvester is 1.6 V and the output power is 0.85 μW with 150 kΩ load resistance at low resonant frequency of 17.6 Hz when the input vibration acceleration was $0 . 1 2 \ \mathrm { g }$ . In addition, the frequency bandwidth is broadened from 0 to 8.4Hz as the input acceleration increases from $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { g }$ to $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ .

1.Introduction

Recently, more and more research reports on energy harvesting for lowpower electronic devices to achieve free from battery power[1-4]. Piezoelectric energy harvesters (PEHs) based on vibration energy harvesting are currently the most studied. With the miniaturization of electronic equipment, piezoelectric energy harvesters have also been required to be miniaturized. For example, energy harvesters are fabricated on a silicon substrate for integration into microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). In order to collect vibrational energy, the substrate of the piezoelectric energy harvesters should be flexible, however, the high fracture toughness of the silicon substrate does not meet this requirement[1,

5].

Another disadvantage of piezoelectric energy harvesters is the narrow bandwidth[6, 7]. For piezoelectric energy harvesters, energy can only be collected when the external vibration frequency is the same as the resonant frequency of the device itself. There have been many studies to widen the frequency bandwidth of piezoelectric energy harvesters[8-11]. One method is to use external forces to change the resonant frequency of the device, another is to control the geometry of the device to change its resonant frequency[12-14]. In addition to the above method, the use of nonlinear vibration phenomenon to expand the frequency bandwidth has also been studied recently [15-21]. However, the nonlinear vibration of the device requires external forces, and the preparation of the device is complicated.

In this study, a cantilever-structure based nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester has a flexible structure, low resonant frequency and wide frequency bandwidth. Firstly, the PZT films were deposited on cantilever-shaped titanium (Ti) substrate via a dip-coating process. The piezoelectric, dielectric and ferroelectric properties of the PZT films sintered at different temperatures were investigated. In This micro-scale devices $( 3 1 \mathrm { m m } { \times } 1 4 \mathrm { m m } { \times } 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ have significant nonlinear vibration phenomenon. It is easy to prepare the device by dip-coating process. In addition, the device does not require any external force to achieve nonlinear vibration.

sections.heading: 2.Experimental
sections.text:
PZT films were fabricated by dip-coating method. $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { C H } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 2 } ) _ { 2 } { \cdot } 3 \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } .$ , $\mathrm { Z r ( O }$ ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 3 } { \mathrm { H } } _ { 7 } ) _ { 4 }$ , and $( \mathrm { C _ { 4 } H _ { 9 } O ) _ { 4 } T i }$ are used as precursor materials, and $\mathrm { C H _ { 3 } C O O H }$ is used as solvent. Lead acetate was added to the acetic acid solvent and stirred with a magnetic stirrer until it was completely dissolved. Zirconium and titanium propoxides are mixed and then added to the lead acetate solution. A 0.4 M $\mathrm { P b } _ { 1 . 1 } ( \mathrm { Z r } _ { 0 . 5 2 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0 . 4 8 } ) \mathrm { O } _ { 3 }$ sol-gel solution was prepared.

A $5 0 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ thick titanium sheet was selected as the substrate, 200 nm thick platinum was sputtered on the titanium substrate. The metal titanium foil with a rough surface is not conducive to the oriented growth of PZT thin films. In addition, in order to prevent the Ti element of the substrate from reacting with the PZT film during sintering, a 200 nm thick Pt was sputtered on the surface of the substrate. The films were grown on both sides of the titanium sheet by dip-coating method, and more details of fabrication of the films are reported elsewhere[22]. In order to optimize the heat treatment temperature, PZT films were sintered at 600- $7 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ .

Large area $( 6 \mathrm { m m } ^ { * } 8 \mathrm { m m } )$ Al top electrodes were evaporated though a shadow mask. The thickness and cross-sectional morphologies of the films were observed by SEM (HITACHI SU 8010), and the crystalline structures of the films were checked by XRD on a Bruker D8 diffractometer. Before measuring the piezoelectric constant, the PZT film needs to be polarized at 12V for $1 0 ~ \mathrm { m i n }$ . The dielectric constant was measured at $1 \ \mathrm { k H z }$ on the HP4294A impedance analyzer.

The ferroelectric properties were obtained by a ferroelectric analyzer system (TF2000, Germany).

In order to determine the transverse piezoelectric coefficient $d _ { 3 1 } ,$ the cantilever was clamped at one end. The cantilever tip displacement was measured by a laser vibrator NLV-2500 (Polytec) under an applied sinusoidal voltage of $V _ { 0 } .$ . The quasi-static displacement $d _ { 0 }$ , the natural vibration frequency $f _ { 0 }$ and the quality factor $Q$ are extracted by a mathematical model. The $d _ { 3 1 }$ is found by the linear fitting of $d _ { 0 }$ and the applied voltage.

The crystalline structure of PZT films sintered at various temperature (600, 650, 700, $7 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ ) were studied. Figure 1 shows the XRD patterns of the PZT films at various sintering temperatures. The PZT film at temperature of $6 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ has a pyrochlore structure. With the temperature rises to $6 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , the PZT film has a perovskite structure. However, the (100) peak and the (111) peak almost have the same intensity, and there is no obvious preferential orientation, it also can be confirmed in Figure 2 (b). Figure 2 shows cross section microstructure images of PZT films at various sintering temperatures. When the PZT film sintered at temperature of $6 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ , there is no columnar PZT microstructure which indicates there is no oriented structure. The PZT film with sintering temperatures of $7 0 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ and $7 5 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ are (100) oriented as shown in Figure 1, the (100) peak and the (200) peak are much higher than the other peaks. In addition, Figure 2 (c) and (d) show the density columnar grains perpendicular to the substrate which indicates there are oriented structure. With increasing sintering temperature from $6 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to ${ 7 5 0 ^ { \circ } } \mathrm { C }$ , the full width at half maximum (FWHM) value of (100) diffraction peak first decrease and then decrease, and the intensity change is the opposite. At the lowest base acceleration level of $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { g } .$ , the dynamic response remains nearly linear. The maximum open-circuit voltage corresponds to the same frequency $( 2 7 \ \mathrm { H z } )$ during the upward and downward frequency sweeps. As the acceleration increases to $0 . 0 8 \mathrm { g } .$ , the device showed a clear softening response as shown in Figure 8b. The resonance frequency is $2 6 \ \mathrm { H z }$ when sweeping frequency up, and the output voltage jumps at $2 1 \ \mathrm { H z }$ when sweeping frequency down. There is a significant bandwidth enhancement in the nonlinear vibration energy harvester. When the acceleration value increases, the soft characteristics of the nonlinear vibration of the system are more obvious. As the acceleration increases to $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g } .$ , the maximum open-circuit voltage (1.6V, 17.6Hz) during the down frequency sweep is more than two times as that of the up frequency sweep (0.66V, 26 Hz). Based on the experimental results in Table 3, it can be found that the frequency bandwidth is broadened from 0 to 8.4Hz as the input acceleration increases from 0.05g to $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ . For a typical cantilever beam structure, the nonlinear vibration characteristics can be exhibited when the length of the cantilever beam is long enough and the thickness is thin enough. It is well known that if the displacement is more than the thickness of the cantilever, nonlinear physics are applied and traditional springmass structure cannot be used. MEMS scale cantilever beam generator are generally fabricated on silicon substrates, with limited length and thickness. For macro-scale devices, generally made of piezoelectric ceramics, so the length and thickness of the ceramic is also limited. So it is difficult to find the nonlinear vibration characteristics of these devices. However, in this micro-scale devices, the piezoelectric layer is a piezoelectric film based on metal material. The device has no limit on its thickness and length, the ratio of length/thickness can be very large. So the nonlinear vibration of the device is easy to realize. ![](images/b9a0dbcd6fa180a927ba083ace78af1f39a76d171e62cfc3596d402b848b1f3e.jpg) Figure 9 Output power and measured load voltages as function of load resistance under an acceleration of $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ Figure 9 shows the output power and measured load voltages as function of load resistance under an acceleration of $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ , when the frequency down sweep to 17.6Hz and the output voltage reaches the maximum under an acceleration of 0.12g. sections.heading: 4.Conclusions
sections.text:
In this paper, a nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester has been fabricated. PZT films were deposited on cantilever-shaped titanium (Ti) substrate via a dipcoating process. The electrical properties of the PZT films sintered at different temperatures were investigated. Results shows that strongly textured PZT films can be achieved at sintering temperature of ${ 7 0 0 } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ which improved dielectric, ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties. The remnant polarization is $1 6 . 3 4 ~ \mu \mathrm { C / c m } ^ { 2 }$ $\mu \mathrm { m }$ , the transverse piezoelectric coefficient $d _ { 3 1 }$ is $- 1 1 . 4 ~ \mathrm { p m V ^ { - 1 } }$ , and the relative permittivity is 311 for PZT films with sintering temperature of $7 0 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ .

The nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester has a flexible structure, low resonant frequency and wide frequency bandwidth. In this micro-scale devices $( 2 5 \mathrm { m m } { \times } 1 4 \mathrm { m m } { \times } 5 0 \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , the piezoelectric layer is a piezoelectric film based on metal material (Ti). So the device has good flexibility. The nonlinear vibration is used to increase the output voltage and increase the bandwidth in the micro-scale devices. This phenomenon is very encouraging, the nonlinear piezoelectric energy harvester has a low resonance frequency $( < 3 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ and low acceleration $( < 1 \ \mathrm { g } )$ with wide bandwidth. The frequency bandwidth is broadened from 0 to $8 . 4 \mathrm { H z }$ as the input acceleration increases from $0 . 0 5 \mathrm { g }$ to $0 . 1 2 \mathrm { g }$ . The normalized power density of this device (35. $. 6 7 \ \mu \mathrm { W } \ \mathrm { g } ^ { - 2 } \ \mathrm { H z } ^ { - 1 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 3 } )$ was obvious higher than the published works. The output power of this device $( 0 . 8 5 \mu \mathrm { W } )$ was lower than others. However, the device worked at low frequency $( 1 7 . 6 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ , and output power can be increased by optimizing the size of the device and electrode, and by improving the piezoelectric properties of PZT films in future work.
